title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
tagline: Cross out multiples to find every prime up to N in O(N log log N).

intuition.analogy: Walk down the number line. The first uncrossed number (2) is prime — now cross out every second number after it. Move to the next uncrossed number (3), cross out every third, and so on. Whatever survives is prime.
paragraphs: Testing each number for primality individually is slow. The sieve flips the logic: instead of asking 'is n prime?', it eliminates composites wholesale by crossing out the multiples of each prime it finds.
Two optimisations make it fast. Start crossing out from p² (smaller multiples already had a smaller prime factor crossing them), and only sieve primes up to √N (any composite ≤ N has a factor ≤ √N).
The running time O(N log log N) is nearly linear — the log log factor comes from summing 1/p over primes. The sieve is the foundation for factorisation tables, Euler's totient, and divisor counts.
intuition.keyIdea: Each prime erases its multiples; survivors are prime. Start at p² and sieve only up to √N.

steps.title: Assume all prime
steps.detail: isPrime[2..N] = true; 0 and 1 are not prime.

steps.title: Cross out multiples
steps.detail: For p from 2 to √N, if isPrime[p], mark p², p²+p, p²+2p, … as composite.

steps.title: Collect
steps.detail: Indices still true are primes. Optionally store smallest prime factors for fast factorisation.

complexity.timeReason: Summing N/p over primes p ≤ N gives the near-linear log log bound.
complexity.spaceReason: A boolean array of size N (bitset halves the memory).

pitfalls: Start the inner loop at p·p, not 2·p, to avoid redundant work.
Use long long for p·p when N is large to avoid overflow.
For a single primality test of a huge number, use Miller-Rabin instead — the sieve needs O(N) memory.

dryRun.clickMoment: When sieving 3, the number 9 = 3² is the first NEW composite it removes — 6 and 12 were already crossed by 2. Starting at p² avoids re-crossing those.

problems.title: Count Primes
problems.statement: Count primes strictly less than n.

approach: The Sieve of Eratosthenes marks multiples of each prime as composite; what's left are primes.
Start from p=2; for each prime mark p·p, p·p+p, … as composite. Count remaining primes below n.

problems.title: Closest Prime Numbers in Range
problems.statement: Find the closest pair of primes in [left, right].
problems.hint: Sieve the range, scan consecutive primes.

approach: Sieve primes up to right, then scan the primes within [left, right] for the closest consecutive pair (smallest difference).
Track the previous prime in range; the first pair with difference < current best wins (ties prefer the smaller pair).

problems.title: Prime Factorization (SPF)
problems.hint: Sieve storing the smallest prime factor of each number.

approach: A modified sieve records the smallest prime factor (SPF) of every number. Then any n is factorised by repeatedly dividing by spf[n].
Precompute SPF once in O(N log log N); each factorisation is O(log n).

problems.title: Distinct Prime Factors Count
problems.statement: Count distinct primes across a product range.

approach: A sieve variant counts distinct prime factors: for each prime p, increment a counter for every multiple of p.
After the sieve, cnt[x] is the number of distinct primes dividing x.

problems.title: Ugly Number / Smooth Numbers
problems.statement: Generate numbers with only small prime factors.

approach: Ugly numbers have only 2, 3, 5 as prime factors. Build them in order: each new ugly number is the smallest of (last·2, last·3, last·5) using three pointers.
Advance whichever pointer(s) produced the chosen value to avoid duplicates.

codes.title: solution.cpp
solution.py
codes.source:
class Solution:
    def nthUglyNumber(self, n: int) -> int:
        dp = [1] * n
        i2 = i3 = i5 = 0
        for i in range(1, n):
            n2, n3, n5 = dp[i2] * 2, dp[i3] * 3, dp[i5] * 5
            nxt = min(n2, n3, n5)
            dp[i] = nxt
            if nxt == n2: i2 += 1
            if nxt == n3: i3 += 1
            if nxt == n5: i5 += 1
        return dp[-1]
